newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-FOUR-WAY U.S. OPEN BATTLE LEAVES THREE CRUSHED LOSERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-FOUR-WAY U.S. OPEN BATTLE LEAVES THREE CRUSHED LOSERS.

text.p: For the thousands of fans at the U.S. Open on Sunday the four-way battle for the championship was thrilling. But for the three players who failed it was an excruciating experience.
As Ernie Els, Colin Montgomerie, Tom Lehman and Jeff Maggert played the final holes on the sun-drenched Congressional Country Club course, the tension was palpable.
Els likened the conditions to a war and the big South African prevailed by playing even-par golf over the last five crucial holes.
Montgomerie bogeyed the 17th, Lehman bogeyed 16 and 17, while Maggert blew up to go five-over on the final six holes.
All three were bitterly disappointed, none more than Montgomerie, the burly Scot who was considered by many the favourite to finally win his first major championship.

"It's getting me down now, this major thing," he said after pacing the clubhouse veranda trying to find a private moment to compose himself. "I cried after the round, sure, I think it's just the emotion of the whole thing and having come close, so close."

Montgomerie, the best golfer in Europe the last four years, looked like an Open winner at Pebble Beach in 1992 until Tom Kite found a answer to the howling wind and claimed victory. He lost to Els in a three-way playoff in the 1994 Open at Oakmont and lost the PGA Championship at Riviera in 1995, also in a playoff.
Montgomerie was still tied with Els on the 71st hole Sunday but missed a five-foot putt for par after pushing a 6-iron into the greenside rough.

He said "a commotion" in the crowd forced a long wait over the putt, and he complained that the 17th and 18th greens -- across a small lake from each other -- were "simply too close" together for major competition.
Lehman, the calm British Open champion, also lost the tournament at the 17th, a spectacular par-4 with a green that is surrounded on three sides by water.
He fired his second shot at the pin on the dangerous hole and found the water instead. A long of agony on his face told the story as the inevitable bogey knocked him out of contention.
"I had perfect yardage, I thought, to a perfect pin," he said of his 7-iron from 189 yards. But he noted, the shot was "easy to catch a hair fat, if you don't watch out, and I did."
Lehman, who has led the Open going into the final round the last three years without winning, did not share Montgomerie's critique of the proximity of the 17th and 18th greens.

"That whole theatre right there and so many people were cheering and pulling for me. It was thrilling. And, I'm just very, very, I guess you would say, bitterly disappointed that I didn't pull it off."
Lehman said he felt he had let the tournament get away.
"I've had a lot of chances and Monty (Montgomerie) has had a lot of chances. We should each have won more, but that's part of really what hurts."
Maggert, who had the lead at the fourth hole and was tied for the top spot for five holes, bogeyed 13, bogeyed 16 then got a disasterous double bogey on 17 to plunge from contention.
"I just got to forget about this week," said Maggert.
That sentiment was certainly shared by the other two golfers who lost the 1997 U.S. Open's war of attrition through those stirring final holes.
